newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa cuts losses late to end nearly flat.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa cuts losses late to end nearly flat.

text.p: LIFFE cocoa futures erased most of their losses late Thursday on short-covering and trade buying to end little changed after prices held key support levels.
July closed up a stg at 995 stg per tonne, off its session low of 981. The 981-level on July was also the May 1 low.
September lost a stg to 1,015. December finished as the biggest loser with a four-stg drop to 1,015.
After fund liquidation and local speculator sales emerged late on Wednesday and this morning, traders were looking for further losses when New York gapped down at the open.
But when selling failed several times to take July through the April 9 low of 980 and September through support at 1,000, selling faded in the afternoon.
Floor sources said the trade bought when July was between 981 and 984 to try to stabilize prices.
That, coupled with local short covering in the final hour of trading after the market showed resilience at key levels, helped cocoa cut its early double-digit deficit, traders said.

Despite the late rebound, floor traders did not expect cocoa's fortunes to mount. They said funds were still net long in London and speculated that more weak longs had to be shaken out of the market before a rally could take hold.
If July breaks 980, traders said prices could drop swiftly because they did not see solid support surfacing until about 950.

Traders said about 3,000 lots were crossed, mainly in September 1997 and September 1998. They also noted switches in July/September as investors rolled positions. July/September widened out to about 27 stg before narrowing again to 20, down two from Wednesday's close.

An estimated 115 against actuals (AA) trades also added to total turnover of 9,924 contracts. Of that volume, July grabbed 3,837 trades and September tallied 3,485. March 1998 was third most active with 1,056 trades.
In options, 10 July 1,000 calls, 10 July 1,000 puts and 10 December 1,100 calls changed hands. But traders said at-the-money implied volatilities slid this week, with July down near 16 percent.
